item.content:encoded:
Like I say above, the first is manifestly the case in terms of the non-canon. The volume of staff casually mentioned on the mainlist can ruin your suspension of disbelief if you think about it all as a single organization simultaneously running all these procedures.

Personally, I also just assumed the third. I imagine The Foundation running in a military model. All new recruits, no matter what their final roles will be, go thru basic training. This is where they learn how to tell who outranks you, how to fill out a time-card, that a red plus is the sign for a med station, that a blue plus is the sign for an emergency meme treatment station, and that opening a door with a red spiral won't get you in trouble because what's inside will make you never have had existed in the first place. For the sake of efficiency and security, you do this in large groups in a very few locations. Since everyone is already all together in one place, secondary job-specific training and orientation happens just after that at the same locations.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
Hmm, yeah…reality check. I currently work for an employer with about 3,000 total employees — actually big enough to have regular group orientations. They have them once a week for new hires (from all departments) and HR presents general information. After that, there is a smaller orientation given by whatever department you work in.

The general orientation usually has 10-20 people in it. So the idea of the Foundation having an orientation for a roomful of agents, tech support people, janitors…whatever…does stretch the imagination somewhat. Unless the Foundation is really huge, or they don't do it very often, and/or orient people at a central site and then ship then off to their actual assignment.

item.content:encoded: The Foundation is bloody HUGE. Even if you only count the people specifically mentioned in articles, The Foundation has more staff than any corporation and most governments; more staff than the population of some countries. Then consider that even the most bottom-rung is spending every day with things that man was literally not meant to know, burn-out is going to be worse than soldiers in active combat. Factor in the personel loss from lethal, mind-breaking, or dimensionally-flinging skips; and I think it's safe to assume that every department needs to recruit at least a handful of new emloyees every week.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
This is an accurate and complete transcript of my "orientation" at a tech support call center in 1996. There were five of us starting that day, all in shirt and tie except for the one guy in khakis and a polo. I remember thinking that he was too informal for a first day. Turns out, I was wrong. The speaker (our section lead) was wearing a T-shirt for a band named "Satan's Disciples", black flip-flops, and jeans so raggedy that I can also tell you he wore red boxers.

"This is where you sit. Don't use the red chairs, they suck. That's Dave. The bathroom is over there. Here's your script books. Don't cuss, the boss likes to piggy-back and you'll get a write-up if you cuss. Do any of you smoke? Dave is always holding."

Dave was relatively professional-looking. He really needed to do laundry, but his t-shirt was funny and I can't tell you anything about his underwear. None of us bothered with the dress code on day 2.

What's my point? "Informal" is relative, and this tale falls well above my personal threshold of realistic characterization. Your mileage may vary.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded: What? Where did I say that the Foundation shouldn't be hiring people regularly? I said people should be replaced on an as-needed basis. Entire units of people don't all get burned out or old all at once. You want to talk about crippling, imagine replacing an entire site's IT staff all at once, en masse, which is what's implied to be happening here. All the institutional knowledge of a professional organization rotating at once would be absolutely devastating.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
While the orientations tend to be whimsical and silly, the sentiment that the Foundation shouldn't be hiring people regularly is even more so.

There's things called burnout and turnover. We don't chain people to their desks; if they are getting worn out to the point where they can't do their jobs, they're better off elsewhere. Not to mention, have you ever worked with a guy who's not old enough to be retiring but old enough that new concepts are hard to grasp for them? That kind of employee can be crippling in the business world. It would be deadly at the Foundation.
